claim: EmrE is a multi-drug efflux pump from Escherichia coli
source: The model multi-drug efflux pump from Escherichia coli, EmrE, can perform multiple types of transport leading to different biological outcomes, conferring resistance to some drug substrates and enhancing susceptibility to others.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript to established literature on EmrE.

claim: EmrE can perform multiple types of transport leading to different biological outcomes
source: The model multi-drug efflux pump from Escherichia coli, EmrE, can perform multiple types of transport leading to different biological outcomes, conferring resistance to some drug substrates and enhancing susceptibility to others.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing both resistance and susceptibility phenotypes.

claim: EmrE confers resistance to some drug substrates
source: The model multi-drug efflux pump from Escherichia coli, EmrE, can perform multiple types of transport leading to different biological outcomes, conferring resistance to some drug substrates and enhancing susceptibility to others.
evidence: This is supported by growth assays showing resistance to ethidium bromide (Figure 2).

claim: EmrE enhances susceptibility to some drug substrates
source: The model multi-drug efflux pump from Escherichia coli, EmrE, can perform multiple types of transport leading to different biological outcomes, conferring resistance to some drug substrates and enhancing susceptibility to others.
evidence: This is supported by data showing harmane triggers proton leak and growth defects (Figure 8, Spreacker et al., 2022).

claim: The C-terminal tail of EmrE acts as a secondary gate preventing proton leak in the absence of drug
source: Here, we show that the C-terminal tail of EmrE acts as a secondary gate, preventing proton leak in the absence of drug.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental approaches including pyranine assays, SSME, and MD simulations showing increased proton leak in Δ107-EmrE.

claim: Substrate binding unlocks the C-terminal gate, allowing transport to proceed
source: Substrate binding unlocks this gate, allowing transport to proceed.
evidence: This is supported by SSME data showing harmane-dependent proton leak and NMR data showing substrate-dependent conformational changes.

claim: Truncation of the C-terminal tail (∆107-EmrE) leads to altered pH regulation of alternating access
source: Truncation of the C-terminal tail (∆107-EmrE) leads to altered pH regulation of alternating access, an important kinetic step in the transport cycle, as measured by NMR.
evidence: This is directly measured by NMR ZZ-exchange experiments showing different pH-dependent rates for ∆107-EmrE compared to WT-EmrE (Figure 4).

claim: ∆107-EmrE has increased proton leak in proteoliposomes
source: ∆107-EmrE has increased proton leak in proteoliposomes, and bacteria expressing this mutant have reduced growth.
evidence: This is directly measured by pyranine fluorescence assays (Figure 3A, B) and SSME (Figure 3C, D).

claim: Bacteria expressing ∆107-EmrE have reduced growth
source: ∆107-EmrE has increased proton leak in proteoliposomes, and bacteria expressing this mutant have reduced growth.
evidence: This is directly measured by in vivo growth assays (Figure 2A, B).

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations of ∆107-EmrE show the formation of a water wire from the open face of the transporter to the primary binding site in the core
source: Molecular dynamics simulations of ∆107-EmrE show the formation of a water wire from the open face of the transporter to the primary binding site in the core, facilitating proton leak.
evidence: This is shown by MD simulations analyzing water path length and connectivity (Figure 5).

claim: The water wire in ∆107-EmrE facilitates proton leak
source: Molecular dynamics simulations of ∆107-EmrE show the formation of a water wire from the open face of the transporter to the primary binding site in the core, facilitating proton leak.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between water wire formation in simulations and increased proton leak measured experimentally.

claim: In WT-EmrE, the C-terminal tail forms specific interactions that block the formation of the water wire
source: In WT-EmrE, the C-terminal tail forms specific interactions that block the formation of the water wire.
evidence: This is shown by MD simulations identifying hydrogen bonds between the C-terminus and residues like D84, T56, and K22 (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).

claim: Antibiotic resistance may be mediated by active export of drugs by promiscuous multi-drug efflux pumps
source: Antibiotic resistance may be mediated by several mechanisms, including active export of drugs by promiscuous multi-drug efflux pumps (Munita and Arias, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The small multi-drug resistance (SMR) family has been found throughout the bacterial kingdom
source: Among these transporters, the small multi-drug resistance (SMR) family has been found throughout the bacterial kingdom and exhibits particularly promiscuous substrate profiles (Brown and Skurray, 2001; Pérez-Varela et al., 2019; Schuldiner, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The SMR family exhibits particularly promiscuous substrate profiles
source: Among these transporters, the small multi-drug resistance (SMR) family has been found throughout the bacterial kingdom and exhibits particularly promiscuous substrate profiles (Brown and Skurray, 2001; Pérez-Varela et al., 2019; Schuldiner, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: EmrE is the most well-studied SMR transporter
source: The most well-studied SMR transporter is the Escherichia coli protein EmrE, which confers resistance to a broad array of toxic polyaromatic cations and quaternary ammonium compounds through secondary active transport (Yerushalmi and Schuldiner, 2000a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature and the extensive body of work on EmrE.

claim: EmrE confers resistance to a broad array of toxic polyaromatic cations and quaternary ammonium compounds through secondary active transport
source: The most well-studied SMR transporter is the Escherichia coli protein EmrE, which confers resistance to a broad array of toxic polyaromatic cations and quaternary ammonium compounds through secondary active transport (Yerushalmi and Schuldiner, 2000a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: EmrE couples the energetically favorable import of protons down the proton motive force to drive active export of antibiotics and antiseptics
source: These transporters couple the energetically favorable import of protons down the proton motive force to drive active export of antibiotics and antiseptics (Forrest et al., 2011; Boudker and Verdon, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on secondary active transport.

claim: EmrE is the archetype for the family of the smallest ion-coupled transporters
source: As the archetype for the family of the smallest ion-coupled transporters, EmrE has become a model system for studying the molecular mechanism of proton-coupled transport and multi-drug efflux.
evidence: This is supported by the extensive literature on EmrE as a model system.

claim: EmrE transport is electrogenic for tetraphenylphosphonium (TPP+)
source: EmrE transport is electrogenic for tetraphenylphosphonium (TPP+) and electroneutral for methyl viologen (MV2+) (Rotem and Schuldiner, 2004), consistent with a 2H+:1 drug antiport stoichiometry (Yerushalmi and Schuldiner, 2000a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established experimental literature.

claim: EmrE transport is electroneutral for methyl viologen (MV2+)
source: EmrE transport is electrogenic for tetraphenylphosphonium (TPP+) and electroneutral for methyl viologen (MV2+) (Rotem and Schuldiner, 2004), consistent with a 2H+:1 drug antiport stoichiometry (Yerushalmi and Schuldiner, 2000a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established experimental literature.

claim: EmrE has a 2H+:1 drug antiport stoichiometry
source: EmrE transport is electrogenic for tetraphenylphosphonium (TPP+) and electroneutral for methyl viologen (MV2+) (Rotem and Schuldiner, 2004), consistent with a 2H+:1 drug antiport stoichiometry (Yerushalmi and Schuldiner, 2000a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established experimental literature.

claim: NMR studies of EmrE protonation and alternating access showed that many more states and transitions have populations and rates that are not insignificant at near-physiological pH and temperature
source: More recently, NMR studies of EmrE protonation and alternating access showed that many more states and transitions have populations and rates that are not insignificant at near-physiological pH and temperature (Robinson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior NMR studies.

claim: Different environmental conditions (pH) or small molecule substrates can shift the relative rates of different microscopic steps and alter the dominant transport behavior
source: Inclusion of these states and transitions in the mechanistic model provides pathways that allow for alternative transport activity, including symport, drug uniport, and proton uniport (leak) (Figure 1). In this model, different environmental conditions (pH) or small molecule substrates that shift the relative rates of different microscopic steps can alter the dominant transport behavior (Robinson et al., 2017; Hussey et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and the free exchange model.

claim: Harmane triggers uncontrolled proton leak through EmrE to an extent that is detrimental to E. coli growth and NADH production
source: This has been confirmed experimentally: a small molecule substrate, harmane, triggers uncontrolled proton leak through EmrE to an extent that is detrimental to E. coli growth and NADH production (Spreacker et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Drug binding to EmrE causes proton release from the C-terminal histidine (H110) in addition to the essential glutamate-14 residues
source: Direct measurements of proton release upon drug binding showed that drug-induced deprotonation occurs at the C-terminal histidine (H110) in addition to the essential glutamate-14 residues that define the primary binding site for drug and proton (Thomas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The C-terminus on one protomer in the homodimer is highly sensitive to the identity of the drug bound in the primary site
source: Additionally, the C-terminus on one protomer in the homodimer is highly sensitive to the identity of the drug bound in the primary site (Morrison and Henzler-Wildman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior NMR studies.

claim: Early solid-state 31P NMR experiments suggested a second, lower affinity TPP+-binding site near the acidic loop residues E25 and D84
source: Early solid-state 31P NMR experiments suggested a second, lower affinity TPP+-binding site near the acidic loop residues E25 and D84 (Glaubitz et al., 2000), which are likely to be in close spatial proximity to the C-terminal tail in this small transporter.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior NMR studies.

claim: E25 and D84 are likely to be in close spatial proximity to the C-terminal tail
source: Early solid-state 31P NMR experiments suggested a second, lower affinity TPP+-binding site near the acidic loop residues E25 and D84 (Glaubitz et al., 2000), which are likely to be in close spatial proximity to the C-terminal tail in this small transporter.
evidence: This is inferred from the small size of EmrE and the location of these residues in loops.

claim: None of the available EmrE structures provide high-resolution data on the conformation of the C-terminal tail and adjacent loop regions
source: Unfortunately, none of the available EmrE structures provide high-resolution data on the conformation of the C-terminal tail and adjacent loop regions.
evidence: This is supported by discussion of limitations in existing crystal and NMR structures.

claim: Early cryo-electron microscopy and crystal structures revealed the unique asymmetric arrangement of the transmembrane helices and antiparallel topology of the EmrE homodimer
source: Early cryo-electron microscopy and crystal structures revealed the unique asymmetric arrangement of the transmembrane helices and antiparallel topology of the EmrE homodimer, but had very low resolution and limited density in the loops and tails (Fleishman et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Early cryo-electron microscopy and crystal structures of EmrE had very low resolution and limited density in the loops and tails
source: Early cryo-electron microscopy and crystal structures revealed the unique asymmetric arrangement of the transmembrane helices and antiparallel topology of the EmrE homodimer, but had very low resolution and limited density in the loops and tails (Fleishman et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Recent higher-resolution crystal structures of EmrE used a monobody that required mutation of three residues in the TM1–TM2 loop (E25N, W31I, and V34M)
source: However, the crystal structures used a monobody that required mutation of three residues in the TM1–TM2 loop (E25N, W31I, and V34M), including E25, and there is limited or missing density for other loops on the open face of the transporter and the C-terminal tail after residue 104.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent crystal structures.

claim: Recent crystal structures of EmrE have limited or missing density for loops on the open face of the transporter and the C-terminal tail after residue 104
source: However, the crystal structures used a monobody that required mutation of three residues in the TM1–TM2 loop (E25N, W31I, and V34M), including E25, and there is limited or missing density for other loops on the open face of the transporter and the C-terminal tail after residue 104.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent crystal structures.

claim: In NMR structures of EmrE, distance restraints are primarily substrate–protein distances within the transmembrane helices lining the primary binding site
source: In the NMR structures, distance restraints are primarily substrate–protein distances within the transmembrane helices lining the primary binding site, and only chemical-shift-derived backbone torsion angles restrain the loops and tail (Shcherbakov et al., 2022; Shcherbakov et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to NMR structure papers.

claim: The most recent NMR structures of EmrE used a loop mutant, L51I, that disrupts the gating mechanism, locking the transporter open
source: The most recent NMR structures used a loop mutant, L51I, that disrupts the gating mechanism, locking the transporter open, and again had limited restraints in the loops and C-terminal tail (Li et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent NMR structure paper.

claim: The only atomic resolution model of the C-terminal tail of EmrE is from MD simulations
source: In such cases, molecular dynamics (MD) has proven to be an excellent tool, and the only atomic resolution model of the C-terminal tail is from MD simulations (Vermaas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior MD simulation work.

claim: WT-EmrE and Δ107-EmrE grow equally well in the absence of toxic compounds
source: Growth assays of MG1655-ΔemrE E. coli cells expressing WT-, Δ107-, or E14Q-EmrE show that all strains grow well in the absence of toxic compounds (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly measured by growth assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the presence of ethidium bromide, a functional transporter is required for survival
source: In the presence of ethidium bromide, a substrate commonly used to assess the activity of EmrE and other multi-drug efflux pumps, a functional transporter is required for survival (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly measured by growth assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: WT-EmrE confers resistance to ethidium bromide
source: This confirms the known resistance activity of WT-EmrE, that E14Q-EmrE is non-functional, and that Δ107-EmrE is properly expressed to the inner membrane, folded and functionally able to confer resistance to toxic compounds in a manner comparable to the WT transporter.
evidence: This is directly measured by growth assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: E14Q-EmrE is non-functional
source: This confirms the known resistance activity of WT-EmrE, that E14Q-EmrE is non-functional, and that Δ107-EmrE is properly expressed to the inner membrane, folded and functionally able to confer resistance to toxic compounds in a manner comparable to the WT transporter.
evidence: This is directly measured by growth assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: Δ107-EmrE is properly expressed to the inner membrane, folded and functionally able to confer resistance to toxic compounds in a manner comparable to the WT transporter
source: This confirms the known resistance activity of WT-EmrE, that E14Q-EmrE is non-functional, and that Δ107-EmrE is properly expressed to the inner membrane, folded and functionally able to confer resistance to toxic compounds in a manner comparable to the WT transporter.
evidence: This is directly measured by growth assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is a small but reproducible growth defect for cells expressing Δ107-EmrE in the absence of exogenous substrate
source: There is a small but reproducible growth defect for cells expressing Δ107-EmrE in the absence of exogenous substrate (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is directly measured by growth assays shown in Figure 2A, B.

claim: The growth defect for Δ107-EmrE becomes apparent around 5 hr, the point at which available fermentable sugars in LB media are depleted
source: This defect becomes apparent around 5 hr, the point at which available fermentable sugars in LB media are depleted, increasing dependence on the proton motive force for energy production (Baev et al., 2006).
evidence: This is observed in growth curves (Figure 2B) and supported by citation to literature on E. coli metabolism.

claim: Depletion of fermentable sugars increases dependence on the proton motive force for energy production
source: This defect becomes apparent around 5 hr, the point at which available fermentable sugars in LB media are depleted, increasing dependence on the proton motive force for energy production (Baev et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on E. coli metabolism.

claim: WT-EmrE in the presence of harmane shows time-dependent growth inhibition similar to Δ107-EmrE
source: A similar time-dependent growth inhibition is observed for WT-EmrE in the presence of harmane, and we have previously shown that this substrate triggers uncoupled proton leak through EmrE (Spreacker et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and growth assays with harmane (Figure 8).

claim: Harmane triggers uncoupled proton leak through EmrE
source: A similar time-dependent growth inhibition is observed for WT-EmrE in the presence of harmane, and we have previously shown that this substrate triggers uncoupled proton leak through EmrE (Spreacker et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: WT-EmrE proteoliposomes show a gradual increase in internal pH over time in pyranine assays
source: WT-EmrE proteoliposomes show a gradual increase in internal pH over time (Figure 3A, solid black), which is faster than the pH change for E14Q-EmrE proteoliposomes (Figure 3A, solid gray).
evidence: This is directly measured by pyranine fluorescence assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: WT-EmrE shows faster pH change than E14Q-EmrE in pyranine assays
source: WT-EmrE proteoliposomes show a gradual increase in internal pH over time (Figure 3A, solid black), which is faster than the pH change for E14Q-EmrE proteoliposomes (Figure 3A, solid gray).
evidence: This is directly measured by pyranine fluorescence assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: WT-EmrE shows a small amount of proton leak
source: This is consistent with a small amount of proton leak through WT-EmrE and a role for E14 in mediating leak.
evidence: This is inferred from the pyranine assay data comparing WT-EmrE to E14Q-EmrE.

claim: E14 plays a role in mediating proton leak
source: This is consistent with a small amount of proton leak through WT-EmrE and a role for E14 in mediating leak.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in leak between WT-EmrE and E14Q-EmrE in pyranine assays.

claim: ∆107-EmrE proteoliposomes show a much faster rise in internal pH than WT-EmrE in pyranine assays
source: ∆107-EmrE proteoliposomes show a much faster rise in internal pH in this assay (Figure 3A, solid red).
evidence: This is directly measured by pyranine fluorescence assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CCCP causes rapid proton leak for all proteoliposome samples
source: Repeating the experiment with the protonophore CCCP in the external buffer results in rapid proton leak for all proteoliposome samples (Figure 3A, dotted lines), and the results match the timescale and amplitude of proton leak observed for the ∆107-EmrE proteoliposomes.
evidence: This is directly measured by pyranine fluorescence assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The proton leak through ∆107-EmrE matches the timescale and amplitude of CCCP-induced leak
source: Repeating the experiment with the protonophore CCCP in the external buffer results in rapid proton leak for all proteoliposome samples (Figure 3A, dotted lines), and the results match the timescale and amplitude of proton leak observed for the ∆107-EmrE proteoliposomes.
evidence: This is directly measured by pyranine fluorescence assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: C-terminal tail truncation causes rapid proton leak through EmrE
source: Thus, C-terminal tail truncation causes rapid proton leak through EmrE.
evidence: This is concluded from the pyranine assay data showing increased leak in ∆107-EmrE.

claim: Both WT- and Δ107-EmrE have measurable current in the presence of a pH gradient in SSME assays
source: In the absence of drug, empty liposomes have minimal charge movement as expected for minimal proton leak. However, both WT- and Δ107-EmrE have measurable current in the presence of a pH gradient, and ∆107-EmrE has consistently higher leak under all pH conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly measured by SSME shown in Figure 3C, D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ∆107-EmrE has consistently higher leak than WT-EmrE under all pH conditions in SSME assays
source: In the absence of drug, empty liposomes have minimal charge movement as expected for minimal proton leak. However, both WT- and Δ107-EmrE have measurable current in the presence of a pH gradient, and ∆107-EmrE has consistently higher leak under all pH conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly measured by SSME shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both WT- and ∆107-EmrE show increased net charge movement at higher absolute pH in SSME assays
source: Both WT- and ∆107-EmrE also show increased net charge movement at higher absolute pH (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly measured by SSME shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The two E14 residues in EmrE have pKa values near neutral pH
source: In symmetric pH environments, the only amino acid side chains with pKa values near neutral pH are E14 (pKa 6.8 ± 0.1 and 8.5 ± 0.2 at 25°C) and H110 (6.98 ± 0.01, 7.05 ± 0.02) (Thomas et al., 2018; Morrison et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior NMR pH titration studies.

claim: H110 in EmrE has pKa values near neutral pH
source: In symmetric pH environments, the only amino acid side chains with pKa values near neutral pH are E14 (pKa 6.8 ± 0.1 and 8.5 ± 0.2 at 25°C) and H110 (6.98 ± 0.01, 7.05 ± 0.02) (Thomas et al., 2018; Morrison et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior NMR pH titration studies.

claim: ∆107-EmrE is lacking H110
source: ∆107-EmrE is lacking Histidine (H110), so any proton binding/release from H110 that contributes to the capacitive current will be absent in ∆107-EmrE, but the net charge transport (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, right, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, D) is greater for ∆107-EmrE than for WT-EmrE.
evidence: This is a direct consequence of the truncation after residue 106.

claim: The net charge transport is greater for ∆107-EmrE than for WT-EmrE in SSME assays
source: ∆107-EmrE is lacking Histidine (H110), so any proton binding/release from H110 that contributes to the capacitive current will be absent in ∆107-EmrE, but the net charge transport (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, right, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, D) is greater for ∆107-EmrE than for WT-EmrE.
evidence: This is directly measured by SSME shown in Figure 3D and supplements.

claim: Δ107-EmrE is in fast-intermediate exchange at both pH 5.5 and pH 8.5 in the absence of drug
source: In the absence of drug, Δ107-EmrE is in fast-intermediate exchange at both pH values, with only one set of peaks and significant line broadening (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly observed in NMR spectra shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The NMR spectra of Δ107-EmrE at pH 5.5 and pH 8.5 are distinct, with slightly more line broadening at high pH
source: However, the spectra are distinct, with slightly more line broadening at high pH.
evidence: This is directly observed in NMR spectra shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Protonation of E14 affects the overall structure of ∆107-EmrE
source: This indicates that protonation of E14 still affects the overall structure of ∆107-EmrE, and alternating access is slightly slower at high pH.
evidence: This is inferred from the pH-dependent differences in NMR spectra.

claim: Alternating access in ∆107-EmrE is slightly slower at high pH in the absence of drug
source: This indicates that protonation of E14 still affects the overall structure of ∆107-EmrE, and alternating access is slightly slower at high pH.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased line broadening at high pH in NMR spectra.

claim: WT-EmrE has similar fast exchange behavior at low pH but significantly slower alternating access at high pH
source: WT-EmrE has similar fast exchange behavior at low pH, but increasing pH results in a significantly slower rate of alternating access (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Morrison et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citation to prior work.

claim: Drug binding slows the dynamics of ∆107-EmrE at both low and high pH
source: Upon addition of a tight binding drug-substrate, TPP+ to ∆107-EmrE at low pH, two distinct peaks become visible for each residue (Figure 4B, red). This confirms that the poor spectral quality of the substrate-free spectrum was due to protein motion and not degradation or aggregation, and that alternating access is significantly slower with TPP+ bound.
evidence: This is directly observed in NMR spectra shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The general structure of Δ107-EmrE remains intact and the binding site has undergone minimal perturbation upon truncation of the last four amino acids
source: The similarity of this spectrum of ∆107-EmrE bound to TPP+ at low pH with the spectrum of WT-EmrE under the same conditions (low pH, TPP+ bound) also provides additional evidence that the general structure of Δ107-EmrE remains intact and the binding site has undergone minimal perturbation upon truncation of the last four amino acids (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of NMR spectra shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At high pH, TPP+-bound ∆107-EmrE shows significant line broadening and partial coalescence indicating faster alternating access
source: At high pH, TPP+-bound ∆107-EmrE shows significant line broadening and partial coalescence of the two distinct sets of peaks in the NMR spectrum, indicating that the rate of alternating access is faster (Figure 4B, blue).
evidence: This is directly observed in NMR spectra shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The alternating access rate for TPP+-bound Δ107-EmrE is 4 ± 1 s–1 at low pH
source: The alternating access rate for TPP+-bound Δ107-EmrE is 4 ± 1 s–1 at low pH, and 17 ± 3 s–1 at high pH.
evidence: This is directly measured by ZZ-exchange NMR experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The alternating access rate for TPP+-bound Δ107-EmrE is 17 ± 3 s–1 at high pH
source: The alternating access rate for TPP+-bound Δ107-EmrE is 4 ± 1 s–1 at low pH, and 17 ± 3 s–1 at high pH.
evidence: This is directly measured by ZZ-exchange NMR experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: TPP+-bound WT EmrE has the same rate of alternating access as ∆107-EmrE at low pH
source: TPP+-bound WT EmrE has the same rate of alternating access as ∆107-EmrE at low pH, but does not vary significantly with pH (Morrison and Henzler-Wildman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior NMR studies.

claim: TPP+-bound WT EmrE alternating access rate does not vary significantly with pH
source: TPP+-bound WT EmrE has the same rate of alternating access as ∆107-EmrE at low pH, but does not vary significantly with pH (Morrison and Henzler-Wildman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior NMR studies.

claim: Truncation of the C-terminal tail alters the pH dependence of alternating access for ∆107-EmrE in both the absence and presence of drug substrates
source: Thus, truncation of the C-terminal tail alters the pH dependence of alternating access for ∆107-EmrE in both the absence and presence of drug substrates, supporting a role for this region in regulating the pH-dependent conformational dynamics of EmrE.
evidence: This is concluded from the NMR data comparing WT-EmrE and ∆107-EmrE.

claim: MD simulations used an NMR structure determined with TPP+ (PDB: 7JK8) as the initial structural model
source: We used an NMR structure determined with TPP+ (PDB: 7JK8) as the initial structural model (Shcherbakov et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the methods and supported by citation.

claim: The C-terminal tail was modeled with CHARMM-GUI for MD simulations
source: Since this NMR structure does not include the C-terminal tail, we modeled it with CHARMM-GUI (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the methods and supported by citation.

claim: In ∆107-EmrE MD simulations, a water chain connects E14 at the primary binding site to bulk water
source: In the ∆107-EmrE MD simulations, we identified a water chain (aka 'water wire') not seen in WT simulations that connects E14 at the primary binding site to bulk water.
evidence: This is directly observed in MD simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: The water chain in ∆107-EmrE enters the protein from the open side near R106A, passing through the triad of A61A, I68B, and I71B
source: It enters the protein from the open side near R106A, passing through the triad of A61A, I68B, and I71B, and then comes into the primary binding site (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly observed in MD simulations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: For ∆107-EmrE, there is a leak state characterized by a much smaller log(S) where the water wire is very well connected
source: For ∆107-EmrE, there is a leak state characterized by a much smaller log(S) where the water wire is very well connected, while for WT-EmrE, log(S) is consistently large.
evidence: This is directly measured in MD simulations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: For WT-EmrE, log(S) is consistently large indicating poor water wire connectivity
source: For ∆107-EmrE, there is a leak state characterized by a much smaller log(S) where the water wire is very well connected, while for WT-EmrE, log(S) is consistently large.
evidence: This is directly measured in MD simulations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The existence of the water chain in ∆107-EmrE is consistent with the enhanced proton leak observed experimentally
source: The existence of this water chain in ∆107-EmrE is consistent with the enhanced proton leak observed experimentally.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between MD simulations and experimental data.

claim: The water wire in ∆107-EmrE is distinct from the ligand entry path
source: This newly found water wire starts very close to the C-terminus and is distinct from the ligand entry path (Jurasz et al., 2021).
evidence: This is observed in MD simulations and supported by citation to prior work on ligand entry.

claim: In the initial structure of WT-EmrE, the C-terminus is floating in bulk water
source: In the initial structure of WT-EmrE, the C-terminus is floating in bulk water.
evidence: This is stated based on the starting structure used for MD simulations.

claim: After equilibration, the C-terminal tail comes closer and interacts with the protein in all three MD replicas
source: After equilibration, we observed the tail coming closer and interacting with the protein in all three replicas (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is directly observed in MD simulations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The C-terminal tail has a salt bridge between D84 and R106
source: The tail has two notable interactions with other parts of the protein, the first of which is a salt bridge between D84 and R106.
evidence: This is directly observed in MD simulations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The carbonyl group of the C-terminus forms hydrogen bonds with T56 and occasionally forms a salt bridge with K22
source: The second involves the carbonyl group of the C-terminus, which forms hydrogen bonds with T56 and occasionally forms a salt bridge with K22 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is directly observed in MD simulations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: In WT-EmrE, the water wire is broken at the triad of A61A, I68B, and I71B
source: In WT-EmrE, the water wire is broken at the triad of A61A, I68B, and I71B (Figures 5B and 6D), suggesting that these three hydrophobic residues may act as a bottleneck for the water wire.
evidence: This is directly observed in MD simulations shown in Figures 5B and 6D.

claim: A61A, I68B, and I71B may act as a bottleneck for the water wire
source: In WT-EmrE, the water wire is broken at the triad of A61A, I68B, and I71B (Figures 5B and 6D), suggesting that these three hydrophobic residues may act as a bottleneck for the water wire.
evidence: This is inferred from MD simulations showing the water wire is broken at this location.

claim: For WT-EmrE, the minimum hydrogen–hydrogen distances of A61A–I68B and A61A–I71B are 2.9 ± 0.6 and 2.8 ± 0.6 Å, respectively
source: For WT-EmrE, the minimum hydrogen–hydrogen distances of A61A–I68B and A61A–I71B are 2.9 ± 0.6 and 2.8 ± 0.6 Å, respectively, and for ∆107-EmrE, these distances increased to 5.9 ± 1.0 and 5.4 ± 1.2 Å (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly measured in MD simulations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: For ∆107-EmrE, the minimum hydrogen–hydrogen distances of A61A–I68B and A61A–I71B are 5.9 ± 1.0 and 5.4 ± 1.2 Å, respectively
source: For WT-EmrE, the minimum hydrogen–hydrogen distances of A61A–I68B and A61A–I71B are 2.9 ± 0.6 and 2.8 ± 0.6 Å, respectively, and for ∆107-EmrE, these distances increased to 5.9 ± 1.0 and 5.4 ± 1.2 Å (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly measured in MD simulations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The I68B–I71B distance does not differ significantly between WT-EmrE and ∆107-EmrE
source: The I68B–I71B distance does not differ significantly.
evidence: This is directly measured in MD simulations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The increased distances in ∆107-EmrE suggest that A61A is moving away, opening a pore for the water wire to form
source: These increased distances suggest that A61A is moving away in the ∆107 variant, opening a pore for the water wire to form.
evidence: This is inferred from the distance measurements in MD simulations.

claim: A triangle larger than 5.4 Å in size is required for a water molecule to fit inside
source: For comparison, the diameter of a water molecule is measured to be around 2.7 Å (Schatzberg, 1967). This means a triangle larger than 5.4 Å in size is required for a water molecule to fit inside.
evidence: This is inferred from the known diameter of water and geometric considerations, supported by citation.

claim: In the most hydrated snapshot of WT-EmrE, A61A takes a conformation more similar to ∆107-EmrE
source: Additionally, the most hydrated snapshot in WT-EmrE showed A61A takes a conformation more similar to ∆107-EmrE and very different from dry WT-EmrE.
evidence: This is directly observed in MD simulations shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A61A rotation controls water wire formation
source: This confirms the role of A61A rotation in controlling the water wire formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between A61A conformation and water wire formation in MD simulations.

claim: The PMF for explicit proton transport shows a deep well near x = 0 Å, where the proton is on the glutamate
source: The resulting PMF (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) indicates a deep well near x = 0 Å, where the proton is on the glutamate, and a transition state near x = 10.0 Å.
evidence: This is directly calculated from MS-RMD simulations shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The PMF for explicit proton transport shows a transition state near x = 10.0 Å
source: The resulting PMF (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) indicates a deep well near x = 0 Å, where the proton is on the glutamate, and a transition state near x = 10.0 Å.
evidence: This is directly calculated from MS-RMD simulations shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In the transition state, the CEC is in close proximity to the pore defined by I68 and A61
source: A conformational snapshot from the transition state shows the CEC (Figure 6C, orange sphere) is in close proximity to the pore defined by I68 and A61 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is directly observed in MS-RMD simulations shown in Figure 6C, D.

claim: The pKa for E14 calculated from the PMF is 7.1
source: The validity of this PMF calculation can be further supported by the pKa calculation from this PMF. The resulting pKa for this E14 is 7.1, close to the experimental value of 6.8 ± 0.1 at 25°C (or 7.0 ± 0.1 at 45°C) (Morrison et al., 2015).
evidence: This is calculated from the PMF and compared to experimental values from citation.

claim: The experimental pKa for E14 is 6.8 ± 0.1 at 25°C (or 7.0 ± 0.1 at 45°C)
source: The validity of this PMF calculation can be further supported by the pKa calculation from this PMF. The resulting pKa for this E14 is 7.1, close to the experimental value of 6.8 ± 0.1 at 25°C (or 7.0 ± 0.1 at 45°C) (Morrison et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior NMR studies.

claim: The bottleneck of proton transport is the hydrophobic gate formed by A61, I68, and I71
source: This supports the hypothesis that the bottleneck of proton transport is this hydrophobic gate.
evidence: This is inferred from the PMF calculations and MD simulations.

claim: The two essential E14 residues in the asymmetric homodimer have distinct pKa values
source: Prior NMR pH titrations of WT-EmrE in the absence of drug-substrate revealed that the two essential E14 residues in the asymmetric homodimer have distinct pKa values (Morrison et al., 2015), reflecting their unique structural environments.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior NMR studies.

claim: Upon binding TPP+, one of the E14 residues is protected from protonation and no longer titrates
source: Upon binding TPP+, one of the E14 residues is protected from protonation and no longer titrates, while the other (E14A) retains a pKa of 6.8 ± 0.1, similar to the drug-free state (Morrison et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior NMR studies.

claim: E14A retains a pKa of 6.8 ± 0.1 when TPP+ is bound, similar to the drug-free state
source: Upon binding TPP+, one of the E14 residues is protected from protonation and no longer titrates, while the other (E14A) retains a pKa of 6.8 ± 0.1, similar to the drug-free state (Morrison et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior NMR studies.

claim: The C-terminal histidine (H110) has a pKa near neutral pH in WT-EmrE
source: The only other titratable residue previously identified in WT-EmrE is the C-terminal histidine (Thomas et al., 2018), which also has a pKa near neutral pH in WT-EmrE.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Several peaks in TPP+-bound ∆107-EmrE exhibit distinctly curved titration paths with transitions in two different pH ranges
source: However, several peaks exhibit distinctly curved titration paths with transitions in two different pH ranges (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) for TPP+-bound ∆107-EmrE.
evidence: This is directly observed in NMR pH titration data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The NMR pH titration data for TPP+-bound ∆107-EmrE is well fit with a global 2 pKa model yielding apparent pKa values of 5.6 ± 0.2 and 7.1 ± 0.2
source: Plotting the chemical shift of well-resolved peaks as a function of pH yields titration curves that can be fit using standard pKa equations. In this case, the data is well fit with a global 2 pKa model yielding apparent pKa values of 5.6 ± 0.2 and 7.1 ± 0.2.
evidence: This is directly measured by NMR pH titrations shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The higher pKa (7.1 ± 0.2) in TPP+-bound ∆107-EmrE is close to the E14A pKa in TPP+-bound WT-EmrE
source: The higher of these two pKa values is close to the E14A pKa in TPP+-bound WT-EmrE, and the residues most sensitive to this protonation event are found lining the transport pore near E14A, supporting the assignment of this pKa to E14A (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with prior data and the location of sensitive residues shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Residues most sensitive to the higher pKa are found lining the transport pore near E14A
source: The higher of these two pKa values is close to the E14A pKa in TPP+-bound WT-EmrE, and the residues most sensitive to this protonation event are found lining the transport pore near E14A, supporting the assignment of this pKa to E14A (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is directly observed in NMR pH titration data mapped onto structure in Figure 7D.

claim: Residues strongly sensing the lower pKa cluster around the C-terminus (R106) and 3–4 loop (includes residue D84) on both the open and closed face of the transporter
source: Residues strongly sensing the lower pKa value cluster around the C-terminus (R106) and 3–4 loop (includes residue D84) on both the open and closed face of the transporter, while the 1–2 loop (includes residue E25) and T56 on the open side of the pore sense both pKa values (left).
evidence: This is directly observed in NMR pH titration data mapped onto structure in Figure 7D.

claim: The 1–2 loop (includes residue E25) and T56 on the open side of the pore sense both pKa values
source: Residues strongly sensing the lower pKa value cluster around the C-terminus (R106) and 3–4 loop (includes residue D84) on both the open and closed face of the transporter, while the 1–2 loop (includes residue E25) and T56 on the open side of the pore sense both pKa values (left).
evidence: This is directly observed in NMR pH titration data mapped onto structure in Figure 7D.

claim: There is no evidence that E25 or D84 titrate in the pH range 5-8 in WT-EmrE or other mutants
source: There is no evidence that these residues titrate in this pH range in WT-EmrE or in other mutants for which we have carried out NMR pH titrations (Robinson et al., 2017; Morrison et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2019), making it unlikely that E25 or D84 titrate in this pH range in the full-length transporter.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior NMR pH titration studies.

claim: Truncation of the C-terminus in ∆107-EmrE could alter the structure, environment, and pKa of E25 or D84
source: However, truncation of the C-terminus in ∆107-EmrE could alter the structure, environment, and pKa of these residues.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural changes observed in MD simulations.

claim: The hydrogen bond between R106 and D84 observed in WT-EmrE simulations is broken when the tail is truncated in ∆107-EmrE
source: Indeed, the hydrogen bond between R106 and D84 observed in the WT-EmrE simulations (Figure 5B, D) is broken when the tail is truncated in ∆107-EmrE (Figure 5C), and D84 and R106 have some of the largest pH-dependent chemical shift changes.
evidence: This is directly observed in MD simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: D84 and R106 have some of the largest pH-dependent chemical shift changes in ∆107-EmrE
source: Indeed, the hydrogen bond between R106 and D84 observed in the WT-EmrE simulations (Figure 5B, D) is broken when the tail is truncated in ∆107-EmrE (Figure 5C), and D84 and R106 have some of the largest pH-dependent chemical shift changes.
evidence: This is directly observed in NMR pH titration data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The pKa of the terminal carboxylate in subunit c of F1F0 ATP synthase has been reported to be as high as 5.9
source: There are relatively few experimental reports of the pKa of the terminal carboxylate in proteins, but it has been reported to have a pKa as high as 5.9 for the partially buried C-terminus of subunit c of F1F0 ATP synthase (Grimsley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on protein pKa values.

claim: MD simulations show the C-terminal carboxylate in WT-EmrE hydrogen bonds with T56 and K22 on the open face of the transporter
source: MD simulations show the C-terminal carboxylate in WT-EmrE hydrogen bonds with T56 (TM 2–3 loop) and K22 (TM 1–2 loop) on the open face of the transporter (Figure 5B, D), but the C-terminus in ∆107-EmrE no longer interacts with these residues (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly observed in MD simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: The C-terminus in ∆107-EmrE no longer interacts with T56 and K22
source: MD simulations show the C-terminal carboxylate in WT-EmrE hydrogen bonds with T56 (TM 2–3 loop) and K22 (TM 1–2 loop) on the open face of the transporter (Figure 5B, D), but the C-terminus in ∆107-EmrE no longer interacts with these residues (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly observed in MD simulations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Residues involved in the hydrogen bond networks anchoring the C-terminal tail align well with residues sensitive to the lower pKa in NMR titrations
source: Comparison with the MD simulations shows that the residues involved in the hydrogen bond networks anchoring the C-terminal tail over the pore align well with the full list of residues that are sensitive to the lower pKa in the NMR titrations, including T56A (TM2–TM3 loop on the 'open' face), V15–G17, I37, Y40, V69, and S72–L73.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of MD simulations and NMR data.

claim: The lower pKa observed in ∆107-EmrE is likely an artifact of tail truncation
source: Thus, although this lower pKa is likely an artifact of tail truncation, this data experimentally supports the importance of the interactions between the tail and the rest of EmrE identified in the MD simulations as important for disrupting the water wire and occluding the E14-binding site.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that this pKa is not observed in WT-EmrE.

claim: For the same ∆pH driving force, Δ107-EmrE has ≈3-fold greater proton leak than WT-EmrE in SSME assays
source: Using SSME, we first compared the inherent proton leak through WT- and Δ107-EmrE in the absence of substrate. For the same ∆pH driving force, Δ107-EmrE has ≈3-fold greater proton leak than WT-EmrE (Figure 8A, D).
evidence: This is directly measured by SSME shown in Figure 8A, D.

claim: Upon addition of 16 μM harmane, there is a large increase in proton leak through WT-EmrE
source: However, upon addition of 16 μM harmane, there is a large increase in proton leak through WT-EmrE and a small increase in leak through ∆107-EmrE, such that this substrate triggers identical total leak through either transporter (Figure 8B, D, Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is directly measured by SSME shown in Figure 8B, D.

claim: Upon addition of 16 μM harmane, there is a small increase in leak through ∆107-EmrE
source: However, upon addition of 16 μM harmane, there is a large increase in proton leak through WT-EmrE and a small increase in leak through ∆107-EmrE, such that this substrate triggers identical total leak through either transporter (Figure 8B, D, Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is directly measured by SSME shown in Figure 8B, D.

claim: 16 μM harmane triggers identical total leak through WT-EmrE and ∆107-EmrE
source: However, upon addition of 16 μM harmane, there is a large increase in proton leak through WT-EmrE and a small increase in leak through ∆107-EmrE, such that this substrate triggers identical total leak through either transporter (Figure 8B, D, Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is directly measured by SSME shown in Figure 8B, D.

claim: SSME-detected proton leak increases with harmane concentration and is saturable in both WT- and ∆107-EmrE
source: This SSME-detected proton leak increases with harmane concentration and is saturable in both WT- and ∆107-EmrE (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is directly measured by SSME shown in Figure 8C and supplements.

claim: A saturating amount of harmane results in maximal signal for WT-EmrE
source: If harmane acts as an allosteric regulator of the transporter that can unlock the secondary gate, then a saturating amount of harmane will result in the maximal signal for the WT transporter as observed.
evidence: This is inferred from the saturation behavior observed in SSME assays.

claim: Addition of harmane decreases the magnitude of the pH change upon addition of CCCP to WT-EmrE containing proteoliposomes relative to empty liposomes
source: This was also confirmed in a pH-detected liposomal assay where addition of harmane decreases the magnitude of the pH change upon addition of CCCP to WT-EmrE containing proteoliposomes relative to empty liposomes (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is directly measured by pH-detected liposomal assays shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: In Δ107-EmrE, C-terminal truncation removes the majority of the secondary gate and key residues in the allosteric site
source: In Δ107-EmrE, C-terminal truncation removes the majority of the secondary gate and key residues in the allosteric site, rendering proton leak comparably independent to harmane (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced sensitivity to harmane observed in SSME assays.

claim: Cells expressing E14Q-EmrE grow equally well in the presence or absence of harmane
source: The cells expressing E14Q grew equally well in the presence or absence of harmane, as the mutation of the primary binding site prevents proton binding in the transport pore and abolishes any proton leak (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is directly measured by growth assays shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Mutation of E14 to Q prevents proton binding in the transport pore and abolishes proton leak
source: The cells expressing E14Q grew equally well in the presence or absence of harmane, as the mutation of the primary binding site prevents proton binding in the transport pore and abolishes any proton leak (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is inferred from the growth assay data and known role of E14.

claim: In the presence of harmane, the difference in growth between Δ107- and WT-EmrE is eliminated
source: In the presence of harmane, the difference in growth between Δ107- and WT-EmrE is eliminated, with significant growth defect for both constructs relative to E14Q-EmrE (Figure 8E, F, Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is directly measured by growth assays shown in Figure 8E, F.

claim: In the presence of harmane, both Δ107- and WT-EmrE show significant growth defect relative to E14Q-EmrE
source: In the presence of harmane, the difference in growth between Δ107- and WT-EmrE is eliminated, with significant growth defect for both constructs relative to E14Q-EmrE (Figure 8E, F, Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is directly measured by growth assays shown in Figure 8E, F.

claim: The in vivo growth data matches the in vitro SSME and pyranine transport assays
source: This in vivo data exactly matches the in vitro SSME and pyranine transport assays, demonstrating the importance of the C-terminal tail in gating and allosteric regulation of EmrE in vivo.
evidence: This is concluded from the consistency between in vivo and in vitro data.

claim: Active transport requires that a transporter is only ever open to one side of the membrane
source: Active transport requires that a transporter is only ever open to one side of the membrane.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of active transport.

claim: Formation of an occluded state is generally thought to be required to avoid transient formation of a channel
source: This is generally thought to require the formation of an occluded state where the substrate-binding site is closed off from both sides of the membrane as the transporter transitions from the conformation open to one side of the membrane to the conformation open to the other side in order to avoid even transient formation of a channel.
evidence: This is a general principle in transporter mechanism.

claim: Sometimes multiple gates regulate a more complex transport cycle
source: Often a single gate is thought to control access to the transport pore, but sometimes multiple gates regulate a more complex transport cycle (Diallinas, 2014; Rudnick, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on transporter mechanisms.

claim: GltPh has a mobile core domain containing the substrate-binding site that moves up and down relative to the scaffold domain
source: This is clearly seen in elevator mechanism transporters such as GltPh. A mobile core domain contains the substrate-binding site and moves up and down relative to the more rigid scaffold domain, effectively transitioning between inward- and outward-occluded conformations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies of GltPh.

claim: In GltPh, a small hairpin domain can open to expose the binding pocket for substrate entry or exit
source: From either of these endpoint occluded states, a small hairpin domain can open to expose the binding pocket for substrate entry or exit.
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies of GltPh.

claim: The hairpin gate in GltPh must close to allow the sliding elevator movement
source: This hairpin gate must close to allow the sliding elevator movement and subsequent gate opening on the other side of the membrane (Reyes et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies of GltPh.

claim: Studies of GltPh have highlighted the evolutionary benefit of a kinetically controlled transport mechanism
source: Studies of GltPh have highlighted the evolutionary benefit of a kinetically controlled transport mechanism and the role of allosteric regulation in opening and closing the gate (Riederer and Valiyaveetil, 2019; Oh and Boudker, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of GltPh.

claim: UapA operates through an elevator mechanism
source: UapA, the xanthine-uric acid/H+ symporter from the Nucleobase-ascorbate transporter (NAT) family, operates through a similar elevator mechanism, and residues outside of the primary binding site have also been shown to regulate substrate affinity, specificity, and transport dynamics, supporting a role for allosteric regulation of the transport cycle (Kosti et al., 2010; Vlanti et al., 2006; Koukaki et al., 2005; Papageorgiou et al., 2008; Diallinas, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of UapA.

claim: Residues outside of the primary binding site in UapA regulate substrate affinity, specificity, and transport dynamics
source: UapA, the xanthine-uric acid/H+ symporter from the Nucleobase-ascorbate transporter (NAT) family, operates through a similar elevator mechanism, and residues outside of the primary binding site have also been shown to regulate substrate affinity, specificity, and transport dynamics, supporting a role for allosteric regulation of the transport cycle (Kosti et al., 2010; Vlanti et al., 2006; Koukaki et al., 2005; Papageorgiou et al., 2008; Diallinas, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of UapA.

claim: Multiple occluded state structures have been identified in MFS sugar transporters
source: In the Major Facilitator Superfamily (MFS) sugar transporters, multiple occluded state structures have been identified, suggesting that multiple gates may regulate the function of these transporters as well and may explain the ability of some transporters in this family to switch between proton-coupled sugar symport and uncoupled proton uniport (Madej et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies of MFS transporters.

claim: Some MFS transporters can switch between proton-coupled sugar symport and uncoupled proton uniport
source: In the Major Facilitator Superfamily (MFS) sugar transporters, multiple occluded state structures have been identified, suggesting that multiple gates may regulate the function of these transporters as well and may explain the ability of some transporters in this family to switch between proton-coupled sugar symport and uncoupled proton uniport (Madej et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to studies of MFS transporters.

claim: Within the SMR family, the QAC transporters, including EmrE, are promiscuous transporters with ≈110 amino acids and a highly conserved C-terminal histidine
source: Within the SMR family, the QAC transporters, including EmrE, are promiscuous transporters with ≈110 amino acids and a highly conserved C-terminal histidine, while the Gdx transporters are selective for guanidinium and are missing the C-terminal tail with a total length of ≈105 amino acids and no C-terminal histidine.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of the SMR family.

claim: The Gdx transporters are selective for guanidinium and are missing the C-terminal tail with a total length of ≈105 amino acids and no C-terminal histidine
source: Within the SMR family, the QAC transporters, including EmrE, are promiscuous transporters with ≈110 amino acids and a highly conserved C-terminal histidine, while the Gdx transporters are selective for guanidinium and are missing the C-terminal tail with a total length of ≈105 amino acids and no C-terminal histidine.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of the SMR family.

claim: The tail-coupling mechanism may be important for maintaining proton-coupled antiport while transporting a broader array of substrates
source: Thus, the tail-coupling mechanism may be important for maintaining proton-coupled antiport while transporting a broader array of substrates, but this hypothesis requires further investigation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the differences between QAC and Gdx transporters.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis has suggested that SMRs may have been the progenitors of the MFS, Bacterial/Archaeal transporters, and drug-metabolite transporter superfamilies
source: However, the existence of a secondary gate in EmrE is broadly relevant as phylogenetic analysis has suggested that SMRs may have been the progenitors of the MFS, Bacterial/Archaeal transporters, and drug-metabolite transporter superfamilies as a whole (Bay and Turner, 2009; Jack et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to phylogenetic studies.

claim: A61 is fully conserved in SMR sequences
source: An analysis of 369 EmrE-related SMR sequences (Brill et al., 2015) shows A61 is fully conserved, while I68 and I71 are highly conserved with valine as the only substitution.
evidence: This is supported by citation to sequence analysis.

claim: I68 and I71 are highly conserved in SMR sequences with valine as the only substitution
source: An analysis of 369 EmrE-related SMR sequences (Brill et al., 2015) shows A61 is fully conserved, while I68 and I71 are highly conserved with valine as the only substitution.
evidence: This is supported by citation to sequence analysis.

claim: D84 is the only fully conserved charged residue other than E14 in SMR sequences
source: D84 is the only fully conserved charged residue other than E14.
evidence: This is supported by citation to sequence analysis.

claim: A61 and K22 are highly conserved across the SMR family
source: A more recent analysis of SMR genes within the Joint Genome Institute's Genomic Encyclopedia of Bacteria and Archaea shows A61 and K22 are highly conserved across the SMR family, while I68, I71, T56, and D84 are conserved within the Qac subfamily (Burata et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to sequence analysis.

claim: I68, I71, T56, and D84 are conserved within the Qac subfamily of SMR
source: A more recent analysis of SMR genes within the Joint Genome Institute's Genomic Encyclopedia of Bacteria and Archaea shows A61 and K22 are highly conserved across the SMR family, while I68, I71, T56, and D84 are conserved within the Qac subfamily (Burata et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to sequence analysis.

claim: A61 and K22 are nearly as well conserved as the GXG motif in TM3 and G97 in TM4
source: A61 and K22 are nearly as well conserved as the GXG motif in TM3 known to act as a fulcrum for conformational exchange between open-in and open-out conformations or the G97 in TM4 that is important for dimerization.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The GXG motif in TM3 acts as a fulcrum for conformational exchange between open-in and open-out conformations
source: A61 and K22 are nearly as well conserved as the GXG motif in TM3 known to act as a fulcrum for conformational exchange between open-in and open-out conformations or the G97 in TM4 that is important for dimerization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EmrE structure and function.

claim: G97 in TM4 is important for dimerization
source: A61 and K22 are nearly as well conserved as the GXG motif in TM3 known to act as a fulcrum for conformational exchange between open-in and open-out conformations or the G97 in TM4 that is important for dimerization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EmrE structure and function.

claim: A61C is not reactive with NEM
source: A61C is not reactive with NEM (I68 and I71 not tested) (Mordoch et al., 1999), consistent with the closed hydrophobic gate observed in the MD simulations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior mutagenesis studies.

claim: A61C has impaired resistance to acriflavine and methyl viologen
source: Although drug binding and transport do not report on hydrophobic gating as directly, A61C has impaired resistance to acriflavine and methyl viologen (Mordoch et al., 1999), while A61L has impaired growth on ethidium (Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior mutagenesis studies.

claim: A61L has impaired growth on ethidium
source: Although drug binding and transport do not report on hydrophobic gating as directly, A61C has impaired resistance to acriflavine and methyl viologen (Mordoch et al., 1999), while A61L has impaired growth on ethidium (Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior mutagenesis studies.

claim: I68W, I68C, and I71W impair growth on ethidium
source: I68W, I68C, and I71W impair growth on ethidium; I68A and I71G impair resistance to methyl viologen; and I61C, I68W, I68C, I71W, and I71C have impaired TPP+ binding (Amadi et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2019; Lloris-Garcerá et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior mutagenesis studies.

claim: I68A and I71G impair resistance to methyl viologen
source: I68W, I68C, and I71W impair growth on ethidium; I68A and I71G impair resistance to methyl viologen; and I61C, I68W, I68C, I71W, and I71C have impaired TPP+ binding (Amadi et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2019; Lloris-Garcerá et al., 2013).

claim: I61C, I68W, I68C, I71W, and I71C have impaired TPP+ binding
